summary: FireAtlas Ukraine turns 25 years of NASA fire satellite records into a fire-risk profile for each of Ukraine's 1,766 communities (hromadas), the level where investment, emergency-service and recovery decisions are made. The challenge asks how to merge MODIS and VIIRS hot spots into one consistent record. We built that series: a gradient-boosting model converts 2001–2011 MODIS counts to the VIIRS scale for every 36 km² cell and month. On held-out test years 2023–2025 it cuts the error of monthly totals from 70.4% to 14.8%, and the 2012 sensor jump disappears. On this series we compute five risk measures per community: amount of fire, months a year needing rescuers, recovery to the pre-war rhythm, most critical months, and the share of area that burns every year. Investors, rescuers, community administrations and recovery funds get answers in seconds in a bilingual web app. The analysis runs up to the line of contact; occupied territory is closed. Every number is reproducible from open data with one command.
details:
The problem: fire risk in Ukraine is priced blind. Ukraine is rebuilding, and every investor, insurer and recovery fund asks the same question about each place: is it safe to put money here? Fire is one of the clearest risks, and it is invisible at the level where decisions are made. In April, 468 of Ukraine's 1,766 communities need firefighters at the same time; in winter, at most 21. Yet forces, insurance and recovery money are planned per oblast and per year, as if risk were spread evenly. One community in Khmelnytskyi oblast needs the emergency service 9.5 months a year; many others almost never do.

Why the data did not exist. NASA has watched every fire in Ukraine since 2001, but with two sensors that disagree. VIIRS sees 3.6 times more fires than MODIS. Join the records and fire seems to jump 2.7 times in 2012, when only the satellite changed. Every trend, norm or risk score built on that record is wrong.

What it does and how it works.

Our breakthrough: one honest 25-year record. We built a model that translates every MODIS month into what VIIRS would have seen, for each 36 km² of Ukraine.

  • It was tested on years it never saw (2023–2025), after being selected on separate validation years.
  • It cuts the error of monthly totals from 70.4% to 14.8% and removes the 2012 jump.
  • 95% confidence intervals come from spatial bootstrap.
  • We report what did not work as openly as what did: the fire season has not measurably shifted, and simple administrative regions describe seasons better than our clusters.

The product: FireAtlas, a fire risk rating for every community. Each of the 1,766 communities gets five measures:

  • Amount of fire. Is this community calm or risky? The riskiest tenth burns 3.9 times more than the calmest.
  • Months needing rescuers. When and how long the community needs the emergency service.
  • Recovery. Has fire returned to its pre-war rhythm? 1,195 communities have, 86 have not.
  • Critical months. The community's own fire season: spring, summer or year-round.
  • Critical share. How much of its land burns every year; in 680 communities it is over half.

Users get answers in seconds. An investor asks "Which communities of Zhytomyr oblast are calmest?" and sees a ranked table, a chart and the map highlighting them. A history slider replays any month since 2001. A research page shows every dataset, method and test result.

Business model.

  • Free for communities, the emergency service and researchers, so the atlas becomes the shared reference.
  • Paid for investors, insurers and funds: portfolio screening, site risk reports, and an API for underwriting and due diligence.

Intended impact. Within a year we aim for FireAtlas to be the shared fire-risk reference for Ukraine's recovery:

  • The State Emergency Service plans crews by month and community.
  • Insurers price fire risk per community instead of per oblast.
  • Recovery funds screen sites before they commit money.
  • Every community knows its own fire season.

Beyond Ukraine, the method works for any country from NASA's global data. As MODIS ends its mission, every insurer, investor and government will need a fire record that stays consistent across sensors.

How it is creative.

  • Harmonization is not the end product. We use it as the foundation for something nobody had: a fire risk rating for every community.
  • A conversation instead of GIS skills. People ask in plain words and the answer appears on the map.
  • Satellites as a recovery indicator. A fire regime back to its pre-war rhythm signals that farming and normal life have returned. A placebo test on pre-war years tells real change from noise.
  • Built for the people who decide. Communities are the unit, not pixels and not oblasts.

Factors we considered.

  • Security. We analyse fire up to the line of contact and close occupied territory entirely. No war-period data is shown there, and force positions are never analysed.
  • Scientific honesty. Models are chosen on validation years and tested once. Negative results are published, and every claim is bounded in a limitations document.
  • Data meaning. A hot spot is any heat source (wildfire, field burning, industry, combat), so we never claim a cause.
  • Fairness. Fire is counted per 100 km², so small and large communities are compared fairly.
  • Accessibility. English and Ukrainian, colour-blind-safe scales, works in any browser.
  • Reproducibility. Only open data, no paid keys; the whole result can be rebuilt from NASA archives.

Tools, languages, hardware and software.

  • Languages: Python for the data pipeline and models; JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web app.
  • Data science: pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (gradient boosting with Poisson loss, k-means, Gaussian mixtures), SciPy (Theil-Sen trends), Uber H3 hexagonal grid, Shapely and GeoPandas, Matplotlib.
  • Web: Leaflet maps, in-browser analytics, an optional language-model chat (OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini with the user's own key).
  • Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP; OCHA community boundaries; OpenStreetMap; Natural Earth; DeepStateMap line of contact.
  • Hardware: a standard laptop; the full study runs in about 25 minutes without a GPU.
  • Hosting: Hugging Face Spaces.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) for coding, writing and translation; every number comes from our pipeline.
